correctness.rationale: The arithmetic v function has prime power values v(l)=l and v(l^e)=l+e for e>=2, and v(ac)<=v(a)+v(c), v(t)<=t. For each odd composite m>=21 factor m=ac with a,c odd>=3 and (a-2)(c-2)>=4, obtaining v(m)<=a+c<=m/2. Check exceptional odd composites 9 and 15 directly: v(9)=5, v(15)=8. For odd prime p in even base b with odd leading digit d>=b/2, reverse s is odd with same base-b length and s<b^L<=2p. If s is distinct prime then v(s)=s!=p; if composite>=21 then v(s)<=s/2<p; s=15 cannot yield prime v, s=9 would require p=5 but 5 never reverses to 9 in any even base. Palindromic reversals are excluded by definition; p=2 inadmissible. Thus no such prime v-palindrome; every base-2 leading digit is 1 and meets the condition. Independent finite check tested 1753 odd primes in base2 and verified small exceptions; unbounded result is analytic.

evidence: Boran et al 2023 prove a decimal classification; it does not cover base2 or every even base. Lemma2.7 v(n)<=n is a useful component but insufficient alone when reverse s>p with s<2p. The extra v(s)<=s/2 for odd composites and parity of s exclude those cases.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Known decimal theorem and weak inequality do not directly imply all-even-base leading-digit obstruction.

originality.rationale: Bispels–Boran–Miller–Sosis–Tsai 2024 Definition 2 and Problem 1 ask which bases admit prime v-palindromes; Table1 records composite base-2 175 but not nonexistence for prime binary v-palindromes. Boran et al 2023 characterize decimal prime v-palindromes and Lemma2.7 proves the weaker v(n)<=n; the new odd-composite half bound and even-base parity/leading digit argument establish an all-length criterion beyond base10. No checked broader theorem implies this condition for all even b.
residual_risks: An unindexed elementary nonexistence proof for prime binary v-palindromes might predate this one.
The leading-digit condition is sufficient, not a complete classification for other even bases; prime v-palindromes exist in base16.

value.rationale: This settles the prime nonexistence question completely for base 2, explicitly requested by the general-base prime existence problem, and excludes an infinite natural family of leading digits in every even base. The argument is a concise structural obstruction motivated by the reversal size and valuation function, not an unmotivated finite table scan.
